items.title: Fruit That Lasts
items.speaker: Rev. Daniel Okafor
items.summary: Fruitfulness is not produced, it is grown — by staying connected to the vine.
body: Roots grow in the dark, unseen — and so does character. Jesus' last extended metaphor before the cross is a vineyard, and in it he gives us the whole architecture of the Christian life: null vine, branches, a gardener, and fruit.

Notice what the branch is never asked to do: null The branch has one job — remain. Every verb of effort in this passage belongs to the gardener. Our culture tells us to produce; Jesus invites us to abide, and promises the producing will follow.
So the question this week is not "what are you achieving?" but "where are you attached?" Fruit that lasts grows from connection that lasts.

items.title: Dry Seasons
items.speaker: Rev. Daniel Okafor
items.summary: The tree survives drought by where it is planted, not how it feels.

items.title: Planted in Community
items.speaker: Grace Lindqvist
items.summary: Nobody grows alone — the first church devoted themselves to four things, all of them together.

items.title: Good Soil
items.speaker: Samuel Reyes
items.summary: The sower's seed never changes — the soil does. A written reflection on receptive hearts.
body: Four soils, one seed. The parable of the sower is really a parable of soils — the seed is constant, generous, almost recklessly scattered. What varies is the ground it lands on.

The path is the hardened heart: null bounces. The rocks are the shallow heart: null without depth. The thorns are the crowded heart — and Jesus names the thorns precisely: null, wealth, and wanting. Not evil things. Just choking things.
Good soil, it turns out, is not perfect soil. It is broken-up, weeded, attended-to soil. Which is hopeful news: null can be worked.

items.title: The Lord Is My Shepherd
items.speaker: Rev. Daniel Okafor
items.summary: The world's most familiar psalm, read slowly enough to be unfamiliar again.
body: We know this psalm so well we no longer hear it. Read slowly, it is startling: null LORD — the maker of galaxies — is *my* shepherd. Not humanity's in general. Mine.
And the psalm's geography is honest: null pastures, yes, but also the darkest valley. The shepherd does not route around the valley. He walks through it, ahead of the sheep.

items.title: Songs in the Night
items.speaker: Esther Mwangi
items.summary: What to do when your soul is downcast and God feels far — the psalmist's surprising answer: null singing.
body: Psalm 42 gives us permission we didn't know we needed: null interrogate our own souls. "Why, my soul, are you downcast?" The psalmist talks to himself instead of merely listening to himself.
And then the strangest line: "at night his song is with me." Faith sometimes means singing from memory in the dark — trusting at midnight what you knew at noon.
